Barash and Golden (2010) investigated awareness and use of PrEP among attendees of a Seattle gay pride event and patients at a sexually transmitted disease clinic. Their findings were published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs. 3. Golub, Kowalczyk, Weinberger, and Parsons (2010) examined the relationship between PrEP use and predicted condom use among high-risk men who have sex with men (MSM). Their study appeared in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 4. Liu et al. 5. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 6. Nodin, Carballo-Dieguez, Ventuneac, Balán, and Remien (2008) explored knowledge and acceptability of alternative HIV prevention biomedical products among MSM who engage in barebacking. Their findings were published in AIDS Care. 8. Galea, Kinsler, Salazar, and colleagues (2011) examined the acceptability of PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy among at-risk Peruvian populations. They identified barriers and facilitators to PrEP uptake in a study published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 9. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 10. Poynten, Jin, Prestage, Kaldor, Imrie, and Grulich (2010) investigated attitudes toward new HIV biomedical prevention technologies among HIV-negative gay men in Sydney, Australia. Their study appeared in HIV Medicine. 11. Liu, Lubensky, Koester, and colleagues (2010) identified barriers and facilitators to PrEP use among MSM participants in the iPrEx study in the United States. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International Association of Physicians in AIDS Care. 12. A systematic review conducted in 2011 highlighted the disproportionate burden of HIV among MSM and transgender women globally. It emphasized the need for additional safe and effective HIV prevention strategies, including PrEP, which has shown promise in reducing HIV acquisition among high-risk populations. 13. The iPrEx study, a randomized controlled trial conducted in six countries, demonstrated the efficacy of daily oral emtricitabine (FTC) and tenofovir (TDF) in reducing HIV infection among MSM and transgender women. The study reported a 44% reduction in relative risk of HIV infection in the intervention group compared to the control group. 14. Studies have shown that awareness of PrEP among MSM has increased over time, with 44% to 74% of surveyed individuals expressing willingness to consider PrEP use. Positive aspects of PrEP include its user-friendliness and potential benefits for serodiscordant relationships, while concerns include side effects, stigma, and potential sexual risk disinhibition. 15. Cost-effectiveness analyses of PrEP programs have varied widely, with estimates ranging from cost-saving to over $300,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) saved, depending on factors such as efficacy, cost, and target population characteristics. 16. Feasibility studies have demonstrated that oral PrEP is a viable intervention in various trial settings. However, issues such as stigma, discrimination, and criminalization of MSM and transgender behaviors must be addressed during implementation. This summary provides a detailed overview of the studies and findings related to PrEP and its role in HIV prevention among high-risk populations.
